title: Toward a Unified Statistical Theory of Multi-View Pretraining for Neural Knowledge Graph Learning
claim: Estimation error shrinks at the m^-1/2 rate, and weighting views by noise level recovers oracle-level accuracy that uniform weighting does not.
layout: 3 panels in a row: line plot, box plot, grouped bar chart
description: Three matplotlib-style plots in a row, labeled (a) to (c). Panel (a) is a line plot of subspace error against sample size m, from 100 to 800. It shows a dashed m^-1/2 reference line and two curves with error bars. The blue curve (linear kernel with isotropic noise) hugs the reference. The red curve (anisotropic noise) starts much higher, near 0.032, then converges toward the blue one. Panel (b) is a box plot of error under three weighting rules. Uniform weighting sits high at about 0.012. Inverse-variance and oracle weighting are both low at about 0.004. Panel (c) is a grouped bar chart of weights for Views 1 to 4 under the three rules, in blue, orange and green. Uniform weights are equal across views. Inverse-variance and oracle weights are concentrated on View 1 and fall off for the later views.
caption: Pretraining simulations.
abstract: Knowledge graph learning offers a powerful framework for representing and inferring structured knowledge, with broad practical applications. Two obstacles limit current methods: labeled triples are scarce for each entity and relation, which makes expressive models hard to train, and scoring functions are designed ad hoc, which limits their generalizability and leaves them without theoretical grounding. We address both obstacles with a theoretically grounded framework, with end-to-end guarantees, that extends and subsumes existing methods. The framework proceeds in two stages: multi-view unsupervised pretraining that integrates heterogeneous sources of entity side information into a shared representation, followed by supervised learning across multiple relation types. We establish a unified nonasymptotic risk bound that combines the subspace recovery error of pretraining and the sample complexity of the labeled data in a single guarantee, quantifying formally how large-scale unlabeled data from multiple views benefits downstream knowledge prediction. Synthetic experiments validate each component of the theory, and experiments on large-scale real-world knowledge graph benchmarks confirm the effectiveness of our approach.
